prime.problem: A bond's cash flows are fixed, but its price swings every time rates move. Two "5-year" bonds can lose different amounts on the same rate move, and repricing every scenario gives no single number to hedge or add across a portfolio.
prime.fits: Third card of the money part. It applies time value of money (price = NPV at the yield) and then asks a new question: how sensitive is that sum to the rate? Duration is the first of the course's three slopes, with beta and delta to come.
expect: price as a sum of discounted flows
prime.goal: Price a coupon bond, compute its durations and DV01, predict a price change from a yield move, and say when convexity or a full reprice is needed.

attend: Why is a coupon bond's Macaulay duration shorter than its maturity, and a zero's exactly equal to it?
How does "weighted average time" turn into "percent price change per unit of yield"?
Why does the duration line always sit below the price curve, on both sides of 5%?
Why is duration fine for 1 bp but noticeably off at 300 bp?
What goes wrong with these formulas when the cash flows themselves depend on rates?

must: Price = Σ CF<sub>t</sub>/(1+y)<sup>t</sup> → each flow's sensitivity to y is proportional to its time t → the price's slope is −(PV-weighted average time)/(1+y) × P → modified duration = D<sub>mac</sub>/(1+y) is the % price drop per unit rise in yield

Coupons return money early → early flows carry weight at small t → D<sub>mac</sub> < maturity (4.6203 vs 5) → a zero has all weight at maturity → it is riskier per unit of price than a coupon bond of the same maturity (4.76% vs 4.40% per 100 bp)

Price is a convex function of yield → the tangent (duration) lies below the curve → duration alone overstates losses and understates gains → the ½·C·Δy² term closes most of the gap (−4.2098 → −4.0927 vs actual −4.0953 at +100 bp)

Duration and convexity are value-weighted averages across bonds → one pair of numbers summarizes a portfolio → DV01 gives a hedge ratio → but only for parallel shifts, so curve twists need key-rate durations
elevated: Callable bonds and MBS get repaid early when rates fall → cash flows shrink exactly when price would rise → the curve bends the wrong way (negative convexity) → closed-form duration is wrong, so desks reprice at y ± Δy (effective duration)
reference: the convexity formula Σ t(t+1) CF/(1+y)<sup>t+2</sup> / P

compress.prompt: Sketch price against yield for the example bond, draw the duration tangent at 5%, and label (1) the slope, (2) the gap, (3) which way a callable bond's curve would bend. Add two sentences on what each number is for.
checklist: price is the NPV of the fixed flows at one yield
Macaulay duration is the PV-weighted average payment time
modified duration is the tangent's slope as a % of price
convexity is the curvature; it makes the actual price beat the tangent both ways
the estimates add across bonds and give DV01 hedge ratios, for parallel moves only

retrieve.q: Explain why duration has units of years and also works as a rate sensitivity, in terms of how each discounted flow reacts to a yield change.
answer: a flow at t is divided by (1+y)<sup>t</sup>, so its % sensitivity to y is about t/(1+y)
the bond's % sensitivity is the price-weighted average of those, which is D<sub>mac</sub>/(1+y)
so the weighted average time (years) is also the % change per unit of yield

retrieve.q: Walk through repricing a 3-year bond with a 6% annual coupon at a 5% yield: price, Macaulay and modified duration.
answer: flows 6, 6, 106 discounted at 1.05<sup>t</sup>: price 102.7232 (above 100 because the coupon beats the yield)

retrieve.q: Your risk system uses duration only. For which moves and which bonds would you insist on convexity or a full reprice, and why?
answer: small moves (1 bp): duration is enough, the miss is 0.000012
big moves: at +300 bp duration misses by 0.99 and even convexity by 0.066, so reprice
long, low-coupon bonds and zeros have more convexity, so duration misses more
callable bonds and MBS: reprice with a rate model (effective duration), because the flows change

compare.q: Duration and convexity vs delta and gamma: what's the same about them, and why does a delta hedge lose money on a jump while a duration-hedged long bond gains on big moves?
answer: same: first and second derivatives of price with respect to one input, used in a Taylor estimate
bond price is convex in yield, so owning it means positive convexity: big moves either way beat the tangent
a short call is short gamma: big stock moves either way lose against the delta hedge (−0.2231 on a move to 105)
the sign of the second derivative decides who gains on big moves

compare.q: Duration is the bond's sensitivity to yields; beta is a stock's sensitivity to the market. How do you get each, and which one can you compute exactly?
answer: duration: a derivative of a known formula, exact given the flows
beta: a regression slope estimated from noisy data (1.374 ± 0.040 for a true 1.3)
both are slopes of a line and miss when the relationship bends or changes

predict.q: Two bonds at a 5% yield: a 10-year zero (price 61.39) and a 10-year 8% annual coupon bond (price 123.17). Which loses the larger percentage for +100 bp, and for which one is the duration-only estimate further off? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: The zero: its Macaulay duration is the full 10 years (modified 9.52), while coupons pull the coupon bond's down to 7.54 (modified 7.18). Repriced at 6%, the zero drops 9.04% and the coupon bond 6.86%. The zero also has more convexity (99.8 vs 67.6), so duration alone overstates its loss by more: 9.52% predicted vs 9.04% actual, against 7.18% vs 6.86%. Long, back-loaded cash flows mean more duration and more bend.
